parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK dispatcher: What are the main tasks you need the service to do for you day to day?

I need the service to help me find which of my drones can get to where a job starts, since I am the one with the legal responsibility to choose the drone and the way it flies. I plan and run the flights as a dispatcher, and several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones. I also sign off a flight before it leaves, and I can call off a flight when needed.
ASK technician: What are the main tasks you need the service to do for you day to day?

As a fleet technician, I keep drones and charging equipment in working order. Day to day, my tasks include adding new drones to the fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, and taking drones out of service for repairs before putting them back. I also send drones to charge.
ASK desk: What are the main tasks you need the service to do for you day to day?

I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which is the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.
ASK dispatcher: How do you define sites, jobs, and flights, and what properties or rules govern them?

Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time, and each of our sites has its own charging pads. Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, while inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where they started. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and a dispatcher decides which drone flies and along which way before signing off and running the flight.
ASK technician: What properties does a drone or a charging pad have, and what are the rules for adding, retiring, repairing, and charging drones?

Drones in our fleet are of several models from different manufacturers, and they differ in how much they can carry, how far they can fly on a full battery, which sensors they carry, and which charging connector they use. Each drone has a home site, and we have a few dozen charging pads at our sites that use specific connector types which are not interchangeable. As a fleet technician, my tasks for day-to-day operations involve adding new drones, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Repairs and servicing are carried out by technicians, and regulators can ask a company to show how its drones have been looked after.
ASK desk: How are flight corridors, zones, sites, and closures structured, and how do closures affect ongoing or planned flights?

Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce closures that can be planned with a start and end time or be sudden, and these closures are often amended during the day. A closure can even come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
